name: Application Load Balancer (ALB)
oneLiner: You pay an hourly rate, then LCUs, where one LCU is whichever of four dimensions ran hottest that hour.
trap: Only the highest dimension counts: new connections, active connections, processed bytes or rule evaluations. A chatty low-byte API can bill entirely on connections and never touch the byte dimension.

name: AWS Client VPN
oneLiner: Two clocks: subnet associations and connected users.
trap: The association fee bills round the clock with nobody connected, once for each associated subnet. Client VPN also consumes public IPv4 addresses, charged at the standard hourly rate on top.

name: Amazon CloudFront
oneLiner: Per GB out to viewers and per 10,000 requests, plus another per-GB charge for traffic heading back to origin.
trap: Cacheable data from AWS origins to the edge is free, but edge-to-origin traffic such as POST and PUT bodies bills at origin transfer rates. Invalidations are free for the first 1,000 paths each month.

name: AWS Direct Connect
oneLiner: Port hours bill continuously while the port is provisioned, then per GB on the way out.
trap: Data transfer in is free, which makes the link look cheap, but port hours run around the clock regardless of traffic. The colo cross-connect comes from your provider, not AWS, and SiteLink adds its own hourly fee.

name: Elastic IP Address
oneLiner: Since 1 February 2024 an EIP costs the same hourly rate attached or idle.
trap: Chasing unattached EIPs used to be the entire optimisation; attached ones now bill at the identical rate. Both land on the PublicIPv4 usage types, so use lineItem/Operation to tell them apart.

name: Gateway Load Balancer (GWLB)
oneLiner: The GWLB itself bills hourly per AZ plus GLCUs, and the endpoints in front of it bill separately.
trap: Gateway Load Balancer Endpoints are distinct PrivateLink-priced resources with their own hourly and per-GB fees. Budget the GWLB alone and you miss a large share of the total.

name: Gateway VPC Endpoint (S3, DynamoDB)
oneLiner: No hourly fee, no per-GB fee, S3 and DynamoDB only.
trap: Interface endpoints for those same two services charge hourly and per GB, which trips people up. Gateway endpoints work from the VPC's route tables only: no on-premises, cross-Region peer or transit gateway access.

name: AWS Global Accelerator
oneLiner: A flat hourly fee per accelerator, plus a transfer premium layered on top of normal egress.
trap: The premium is charged on the dominant direction only, so an upload-heavy app pays on inbound bytes it assumed were free. It sits on top of standard EC2 data transfer out, never in place of it.

name: AWS Ground Station
oneLiner: Antenna minutes, rounded up, for the contact you put on the schedule.
trap: Calling CancelContact mid-pass does not stop the meter. AWS bills the full originally scheduled duration unless you book a duplicate contact on the same ground station covering the rest, and gaps between them still bill.

name: Internet Gateway
oneLiner: The gateway is free. Egress through it is not.
trap: No line item says internet gateway. Outbound lands on DataTransfer-Out-Bytes against the sending service. Inbound really is free, unlike NAT gateway processing, and egress-only IGW carries no fee at all.

name: AWS Local Zones
oneLiner: Turning a Local Zone on costs nothing.
trap: Resources deployed into a Local Zone are priced on their own scale, not the parent Region's, and data transfer in and out is charged at Local Zone specific rates. Filter the pricing pages by zone before you estimate.

name: NAT Gateway
oneLiner: An hourly fee for existing, then a per-GB fee on everything that passes through.
trap: Data processing is charged in both directions at the same rate. Inbound is not free here, and the fee stacks on top of ordinary data transfer out when the traffic is headed for the internet.

name: Network Load Balancer (NLB)
oneLiner: Long-lived TCP flows drive this one. Hourly fee plus NLCUs, with flows counted as a dimension.
trap: One of three dimensions wins each hour: new flows, peak concurrent flows or processed bytes. Concurrent flows are sampled every minute, so idle-but-open connections bill even with almost no traffic.

name: AWS PrivateLink Interface VPC Endpoint
oneLiner: Hourly per endpoint per AZ, plus per GB processed. The AZ count is the multiplier people forget.
trap: The hourly charge runs for every AZ the endpoint is provisioned in, irrespective of the state of its association with the service. Data processing applies in both directions and tiers across a whole Region.

name: Public IPv4 Address
oneLiner: Public IPv4 now costs by the hour, in use or idle.
trap: The charge reaches EC2, RDS, ELB, EKS, EMR, ECS, Global Accelerator and Site-to-Site VPN endpoints. Addresses you bring under BYOIP are exempt and IPv6 is free, which is the whole point of the charge.

name: Amazon Route 53
oneLiner: DNS queries are genuinely a per-request charge here. Hosted zones bill monthly and Resolver ENIs bill hourly.
trap: Alias records pointing at ELB, CloudFront, API Gateway and similar AWS targets answer for free, and private hosted zone queries cost nothing extra. Resolver endpoint ENIs bill hourly at any query volume.

name: AWS Site-to-Site VPN
oneLiner: Billed per connection-hour while the tunnel is provisioned and available.
trap: An idle tunnel bills the same as a busy one because the meter tracks state, not packets. No VPN-specific per-GB fee exists; bytes land on standard data transfer, and the tunnel IPs draw public IPv4 charges.

name: AWS Transit Gateway
oneLiner: Every attachment bills hourly, and traffic sent into the gateway bills per GB.
trap: The hourly attachment fee runs at zero traffic. Data processing is charged to whoever sends into the gateway, and traffic arriving from a peering attachment is not processed-charged a second time.

name: Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (VPC)
oneLiner: Nothing bills for the VPC itself. Every charge you trace back to it belongs to something you attached.
trap: People search for a VPC line item and find none. The spend is NAT gateways, interface endpoints, public IPv4 hours and cross-AZ transfer, each metered under its own usage type.

name: Amazon VPC Peering
oneLiner: Creating the peering costs nothing. Bytes that cross an AZ or a Region boundary do.
trap: Traffic staying inside one AZ is free even across accounts. Cross-AZ is metered on both sides, so one GB shows up twice. AWS split those out under VpcPeering usage types in early 2025. Cross-Region bills the sender.

name: AWS Wavelength
oneLiner: Nothing for Wavelength itself; you pay EC2 and EBS at Wavelength Zone rates.
trap: Hunting for a Wavelength line item is wasted effort. Cost surfaces as EC2 and EBS usage priced differently from the parent Region, and Wavelength Zones offer only On-Demand instances plus Savings Plans.
